In [[probability]] and [[statistics]], the '''Kumaraswamy's double bounded distribution''' is a family of [[continuous probability distribution]]s defined on the interval (0,1). It is similar to the [[beta distribution]], but much simpler to use especially in simulation studies since its [[probability density function]], [[cumulative distribution function]] and quantile functions can be expressed in [[closed-form solution|closed form]]. This distribution was originally proposed by [[Poondi Kumaraswamy]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Kumaraswamy|first=P.|date=1980|title=A generalized probability density function for double-bounded random processes|journal=Journal of Hydrology|volume=46|issue=1–2|pages=79–88|doi=10.1016/0022-1694(80)90036-0|issn=0022-1694|bibcode=1980JHyd...46...79K}}</ref> for variables that are lower and upper bounded with a zero-inflation. In this first article of the distribution, the natural lower bound of zero for rainfall was modelled using a discrete probability, as rainfall in many places, especially in tropics, has significant nonzero probability. This discrete probability is now called zero-inflation. This was extended to inflations at both extremes [0,1] in the work of Fletcher and Ponnambalam.<ref name=FP1>{{Cite journal|last1=Fletcher|first1=S.G.|last2=Ponnambalam|first2=K.|date=1996|title=Estimation of reservoir yield and storage distribution using moments analysis|journal=Journal of Hydrology|volume=182|issue=1–4|pages=259–275|doi=10.1016/0022-1694(95)02946-x|issn=0022-1694|bibcode=1996JHyd..182..259F}}</ref> A good example for inflations at extremes are the probabilities of full and empty reservoirs and are important for reservoir design.

==Characterization==

===Probability density function===
The [[probability density function]] of the Kumaraswamy distribution without considering any inflation is

:<math> f(x; a,b) = a b x^{a-1}{ (1-x^a)}^{b-1},  \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ x \in (0,1),</math>

and where ''a'' and ''b'' are non-negative [[shape parameter]]s.

===Cumulative distribution function===
The [[cumulative distribution function]] is

:<math>F(x; a,b)=\int_{0}^{x}f(\xi; a,b) d\xi = 1-(1-x^a)^b.\ </math>

===Quantile function===
The inverse cumulative distribution function (quantile function) is

:<math>F^{-1}(y; a,b)=(1-(1-y)^\frac{1}{b})^\frac{1}{a}. \ </math>

===Generalizing to arbitrary interval support===
In its simplest form, the distribution has a support of (0,1).  In a more general form, the normalized variable ''x'' is replaced with the unshifted and unscaled variable ''z'' where:

:<math> x = \frac{z-z_{\text{min}}}{z_{\text{max}}-z_{\text{min}}} , \qquad z_{\text{min}} \le z \le z_{\text{max}}. \,\!</math>

==Properties==
The raw [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] of the Kumaraswamy distribution are given by:<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Lemonte|first=Artur J.|date=2011|title=Improved point estimation for the Kumaraswamy distribution|journal=Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation|volume=81|issue=12|pages=1971–1982|doi=10.1080/00949655.2010.511621|issn=0094-9655}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=CRIBARI-NETO|first1=FRANCISCO|last2=SANTOS|first2=JÉSSICA|date=2019|title=Inflated Kumaraswamy distributions|journal=Anais da Academia Brasileira de Ciências|volume=91|issue=2|article-number=e20180955|doi=10.1590/0001-3765201920180955|pmid=31141016|issn=1678-2690|doi-access=free|s2cid=169034252 |url=http://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/74cf/6193ee129558fb0f7d03835852e1cdd72452.pdf}}</ref>

:<math>m_n = \frac{b\Gamma(1+n/a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(1+b+n/a)} = bB(1+n/a,b)\,</math>

where ''B'' is the [[Beta function]] and Γ(.) denotes the [[Gamma function]]. The variance, [[skewness]], and [[excess kurtosis]] can be calculated from these raw moments. For example, the variance is:

:<math>\sigma^2=m_2-m_1^2.</math>

The [[Entropy (information theory)|Shannon entropy]] (in nats) of the distribution is:<ref>{{cite book |last1=Michalowicz |first1=Joseph Victor |last2=Nichols |first2=Jonathan M. |last3=Bucholtz |first3=Frank |title=Handbook of Differential Entropy |date=2013 |publisher=Chapman and Hall/CRC |isbn=978-1-4665-8317-7 |page=100}}</ref>

:<math>H=\left(1\!-\!\tfrac{1}{b}\right)+\left(1\!-\!\tfrac{1}{a}\right)H_b-\ln(ab)</math>

where <math>H_i</math> is the [[harmonic number]] function.

==Relation to the Beta distribution==
The Kumaraswamy distribution is closely related to Beta distribution.<ref name=FP2>{{Cite journal|last=Jones|first=M.C.|date=2009|title=Kumaraswamy's distribution: A beta-type distribution with some tractability advantages|journal=Statistical Methodology|volume=6|issue=1|pages=70–81|doi=10.1016/j.stamet.2008.04.001|issn=1572-3127}}</ref>
Assume that ''X''<sub>a,b</sub> is a Kumaraswamy distributed [[random variable]] with parameters ''a'' and ''b''.
Then ''X''<sub>a,b</sub> is the ''a''-th root of a suitably defined Beta distributed random variable.
More formally, Let ''Y''<sub>1,b</sub> denote a [[Beta distribution|Beta distributed]] random variable with parameters <math>\alpha=1</math> and <math>\beta=b</math>.
One has the following relation between ''X''<sub>a,b</sub> and ''Y''<sub>1,b</sub>.

:<math>X_{a,b}=Y^{1/a}_{1,b},</math>

with equality in distribution.

:<math>\operatorname{P}\{X_{a,b}\le x\}=\int_0^x ab t^{a-1}(1-t^a)^{b-1}dt=
\int_0^{x^a} b(1-t)^{b-1}dt=\operatorname{P}\{Y_{1,b}\le x^a\}
=\operatorname{P}\{Y^{1/a}_{1,b}\le x\}
.</math>

One may introduce generalised Kumaraswamy distributions by considering random variables of the form
<math>Y^{1/\gamma}_{\alpha,\beta}</math>, with <math>\gamma>0</math> and where <math>Y_{\alpha,\beta}</math>
denotes a Beta distributed random variable with parameters <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math>.
The raw [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] of this generalized Kumaraswamy distribution are given by:
:<math>m_n = \frac{\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)\Gamma(\alpha+n/\gamma)}{\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\alpha+\beta+n/\gamma)}.</math>

Note that we can re-obtain the original moments setting <math>\alpha=1</math>, <math>\beta=b</math> and <math>\gamma=a</math>.
However, in general, the cumulative distribution function does not have a closed form solution.

==Related distributions==
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(1,1)\,</math> then <math> X \sim U(0,1)\,</math> ([[Uniform distribution (continuous)|Uniform distribution]])
*If <math> X \sim U(0,1) \,</math>  then <math> {\left( 1-X^{\tfrac{1}{b}}  \right)}^{ \tfrac{1}{a}} \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a,b) \,</math><ref name=FP2 />
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Beta}(1,b) \, </math> ([[Beta distribution]]) then <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(1,b)\,</math>
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Beta}(a,1) \, </math> ([[Beta distribution]]) then <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a,1)\,</math>
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a,1)\,</math> then <math> (1-X) \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(1, a)\,</math>
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(1,a)\,</math> then <math> (1-X) \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a, 1)\,</math>
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a,1)\,</math> then <math> -\log(X) \sim \textrm{Exponential}(a)\,</math>
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(1,b)\,</math> then <math> -\log(1-X) \sim \textrm{Exponential}(b)\,</math>
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a,b)\,</math> then <math> X \sim \textrm{GB1}(a, 1, 1, b)\,</math>, the [[Generalized Beta distribution#Related distributions|generalized beta distribution of the first kind]]
*If <math> X \sim \textrm{Kumaraswamy}(a,b)\,</math> then <math> \left\{\frac{1}{1-X} \right\} \sim \textrm{MK}(a, b)\,</math>, the [[Modified Kumaraswamy distribution#Related distributions|Modified Kumaraswamy distribution]].



==Example==
An example of the use of the Kumaraswamy distribution is the storage volume of a reservoir of capacity ''z'' whose upper bound is ''z''<sub>max</sub> and lower bound is 0, which is also a natural example for having two inflations as many reservoirs have nonzero probabilities for both empty and full reservoir states.<ref name=FP1 />
